label: Caterina, mother of Leonardo
died: 1494 (if the Caterina of the Milan notes)
summary: Named as Leonardo's mother in the 1457 catasto declaration ('nato di lui e della Chaterina'). Her identity beyond the name is debated.

value.text: Named 'Chaterina' as the mother in the 1457 catasto

claims.statement: The 1457 catasto of Antonio da Vinci describes Leonardo as born of ser Piero 'e della Chaterina'. The document names her only by first name.

value.text: Caterina di Meo Lippi, an orphan from the Vinci area, born c.1436

claims.statement: Martin Kemp and Giuseppe Pallanti (Mona Lisa: The People and the Painting, Oxford University Press, 2017) identify her as Caterina di Meo Lippi, an orphaned girl of about 15 in 1451, from tax records of Vinci. Elisabetta Ulivi (2017) found the argument weak and proposed other candidates.

sources.cite: Kemp and Pallanti, Mona Lisa: The People and the Painting (Oxford University Press, 2017). Cited as the place to check; not read in this session.

value.text: Caterina, a Circassian slave freed in Florence on 2 November 1452

claims.statement: Carlo Vecce (2023, with the novel Il sorriso di Caterina, Giunti) identifies her with a Circassian slave Caterina freed by a Latin act of manumission dated 2 November 1452 and drawn up by ser Piero as notary, with further papers on her ownership and her work as a wet nurse in 1450. The act is a document; its link to Leonardo's mother is Vecce's argument. Press reports say the findings were not yet published in a peer reviewed venue; Finestre sull'Arte notes no document ties the 1452 deed unambiguously to Leonardo's mother.

value.text: Caterina di Antonio di Cambio, or a domestic slave

claims.statement: Elisabetta Ulivi (2017) proposed Caterina di Antonio di Cambio as an alternative candidate and considered a slave origin possible.

claims.statement: Leonardo noted in Milan the arrival of a Caterina on 16 July 1493 (Codex Forster III, f. 88r per one transcription). Later notes list burial expenses for a Caterina.

value.text: The Caterina of the Milan notes was Leonardo's mother

claims.statement: That the Caterina who came to Milan in 1493 and was buried at Leonardo's expense was his mother is an identification made by many biographers (including Kemp) on circumstantial grounds; others read her as a housekeeper.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Caterina di Meo Lippi. Background only, not a ground. Seen in a web search result summary only; the page was not opened in this session.

value.text: 26 June 1494, Milan (if the Caterina of the Milan death record)

claims.statement: A Latin entry in the Milan death registers (Archivio di Stato di Milano), dated 26 June 1494, records the death of a Caterina from Florence, reportedly of malaria. Its link to Leonardo's mother rests on the identification above.

sources.cite: Gingko Edizioni, Caterina tag page (cites the Milan record of 26 June 1494). Seen in a web search result summary only; the page was not opened in this session.

value.text: Married Antonio di Piero Buti, called Accattabriga

claims.statement: Biographies report that after Leonardo's birth Caterina married Antonio di Piero Buti del Vacca, known as Accattabriga, of Campo Zeppi near Vinci. Holds for the di Meo Lippi line; the Vecce thesis also places her in this marriage.

sources.cite: Kemp and Pallanti 2017; Vecce 2023 press coverage. Model recall, not checked in this session.

open_questions: Which candidate (di Meo Lippi, the Circassian slave of the 2 November 1452 act, di Antonio di Cambio) fits all documents? Holders: Kemp and Pallanti 2017 (di Meo Lippi); Vecce 2023 (Circassian slave); Ulivi 2017 (other candidates).
Is the Caterina of the Milan notes of 1493 to 1494 the same woman as the mother? This is an interpretation in all current literature.
